clusters.title: Correlation, parlays and player-prop combos
clusters.decision: Do we price multi-leg bets with measured joint outcomes (and a published correlation matrix), or refuse to publish parlay edges at all?

questions.question: Are parlay legs independent?
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: Which correlation values must origination respect?
questions.answer: See the leaderboard page correlation table.

questions.question: Are same-game parlay legs correlated enough to change the price?
questions.answer: Yes. QB passing yards vs WR1 receiving yards r = +0.562; the four-leg same-team joint probability is 11.1% against 5.7% under independence, so pricing the legs independently understates the joint by a factor of about two.
questions.gap: The correlation's uncertainty, and whether the Gaussian copula parameter is stable across seasons. No interval is published.
questions.how: Bootstrap the pairwise coefficients by season and by team, then propagate the interval into the SGP price.

questions.question: Do the published correlations reproduce from a clean checkout?
questions.answer: Partly. The signs and magnitudes reproduce; the sample size does not (7,560 published vs 6,024 recomputed) because the committed extract covers 2015-2026 while the published coefficients used 2012-2026. The project records this as 'DIFFERS (expected)'.
questions.gap: Whether any conclusion changes at the smaller n. The joint-vs-product gap holds within tolerance (11.14% vs 10.94%, 5.69% vs 5.55%).
questions.how: Re-run the analysis on the committed extract and republish the n, or commit the extract the coefficients were measured on.

questions.question: Can Gaussian copula correlation edge beat sportsbook Same-Game Parlay pricing?
questions.answer: QB pass yds <-> WR1 rec yds r=0.564 gives 34.54% true joint probability (+190 fair) vs naive +300 (25%), but DraftKings KB0010683 confirms books already embed correlation haircuts.
questions.gap: Live quoted SGP payouts vs copula fair value across multiple books.

questions.gap: Historical prop prices, so the gap is a pricing fact, not yet a profit.
questions.how: Publish the pricing gap, and do not quote an independent-leg parlay ROI.

questions.question: Would a correlated-parlay strategy be profitable at real, available prices?
questions.answer: Unknown. The pricing gap is measured; the available price is not.
questions.gap: Available same-game-parlay prices and the operator's correlation policy (terms change).
questions.how: Read the operator's current same-game-parlay terms; do not assume they ignore correlation.

questions.question: Are same-game parlay legs independent?
questions.answer: No. QB→WR1 r=0.562 (n=7560); WR1↔WR2 r=0.120; home-cover vs over φ=0.016. 4-leg same-team joint 11.1% vs product 5.7% — independence understates joint rate by factor ~1.95.
questions.gap: Pearson r between per-team-game quantities (QB passing yards, WR1/WR2 receiving yards, RB rushing yards, home cover vs over)

questions.answer: 23,844 settled tickets.

questions.question: Is the ATS market exploitable by simple public angles?
questions.answer: Under the published pooled test, 'no', but that test is an arithmetic identity (FL-DH-01). Under the one-sided test, the home cover rate is 48.91% with a 95% CI of 47.73-50.09% on 6,892 games, two-sided p = 0.073. That is inconclusive, not zero.
questions.gap: Whether a specific angle is exploitable. 12 classic angles were screened and none survived Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.10.
questions.how: Keep the one-sided test; add a per-angle table with the one-sided CI and the corrected p, and publish the intervals next to the point estimates.

questions.question: Which settlement rulebook governs every backtest?
questions.answer: The repository cites a DraftKings Massachusetts filing (8.1.24) that the regulator lists as obsolete; the active edition is the one approved 10.7.26. Push handling, void legs and minimum leg counts differ by operator.
questions.gap: Which operator, and therefore which rulebook, is the standard. Also unknown: whether the 10.7.26 PDF text matches the old edition on the rules that matter (it could not be fetched in the sandbox).
questions.how: A reviewer decision: pick one operator's filed rules as the standard, record the edition, and re-price the backtest if it changes.

questions.question: Is the gate screen itself working?
questions.answer: Untested. Two controls exist and both fail, so the screen has never been shown to pass anything. A screen that cannot pass a bettor who knows the result is not evidence about real candidates.
questions.gap: Whether the gates are mis-wired. The clairvoyant positive control has not been run.
questions.how: Add a clairvoyant control (bet the actual winner at the stored price) and require it to pass. If it fails, fix the gates before reading any verdict.

questions.question: Does any candidate strategy pass the ten gates?
questions.answer: No. 0 of 23 variants tested in this session and 0 of 9 published candidates.
questions.gap: A candidate that survives G1 (see Q-11).
questions.how: Do not fund, publish a pick, or build a ledger on top of these candidates.

questions.question: Is the spread market exploitable on average?
questions.answer: No. 13,784 settled spread team-games; pooled cover rate 50.0%; binomial p vs 50% = 1.0. Blind backing of any side loses to vig (home -4.89% at stored prices).
questions.gap: Pooled ATS coin-flip test over all settled spread bets with push-aware settlement at closing prices
questions.how: Re-settle from games.csv.gz with spread_line sign convention proved (positive = home favoured, corr 0.425) and moneyline cross-check.

method: Each hub's own decision-readiness register is read as-is and normalised to three states: answered (the hub records an answer and no gap), partially answered (an answer and a stated gap), unanswered (a stated gap and no answer). A cluster is only 'closed' when no hub has an open item in it; disagreement between hubs is shown side by side, never averaged.
